title: The league of the virtuous
hookLine: as a young man he joins a pact of Meccan clans to defend anyone wronged, which he later praised

cards: A trader from Yemen has sold his goods in Mecca to a powerful man, and the man won't pay. The stranger has no clan in the city, nobody to call on.
So, later sirah books say, he climbs a hill near the Ka'ba and calls out his complaint in verse, loud enough for the gathered men of Quraysh to hear.
It's a gamble: shouting into a town where belonging protects you, and he belongs to no one there. Today: Hilf al-Fudul.

teach.h: CLANS MEET AT IBN JUD'AN'S HOUSE.
teach.b: Someone hears him. In Ibn Ishaq's account, several clans of Quraysh gather at the house of a man named Abdullah ibn Jud'an. There they make a pact.
They swear that whenever anyone in Mecca is wronged, whether from the city or a stranger, they will stand together on that person's side until what was taken is returned.
And the later books say they went straight to the man who wouldn't pay, and made him pay. The pact came to be called the Hilf al-Fudul: the league of the virtuous, or the league of the excellent.

Among those present, the sirah says, was the young Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Hold that against this week. In a town where your clan was your protection, here was a promise to protect people with no clan at all.
And he didn't forget it. Years later, after the revelation, he spoke of that day.

The sirah reports him saying he had witnessed a pact in the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an that he would not trade for a herd of red camels, prize animals, and that if he were called to it even now, in Islam, he would answer.
A promise made before Islam, among men who still prayed to idols, and he says he'd keep it.

Teachers draw a lesson from that: a just promise is worth keeping, whoever first made it. The Qur'an later commands believers to stand firm for justice, as witnesses for God, even against themselves or their kin.
The young man in Ibn Jud'an's house had already seen what that looked like.

how: Muslim teachers cite the Hilf al-Fudul as an example of the Prophet ﷺ honoring a just pact made before Islam, and it is invoked in discussions of justice and of working with others for the common good.

the virtuous: a pact to stand with anyone wronged
the chiefs of Quraysh who held the Ka'ba

games.q: you're a stranger in Mecca. a powerful man has your goods and won't pay. you have no clan in the city. what do you do?
o: call out your complaint from a hill by the Ka'ba.
games.why: later sirah books say he cried out in verse; clans of Quraysh made a pact and got him his due.

practice: Let one face come: someone near you who is the stranger on the hill right now, a coworker blamed for another's mistake, a neighbor being talked about, a person owed something they can't collect.

Ask quietly what one thing would put you on their side, not a grand rescue, just a word, a witness, a seat beside them, and hold it until it feels possible. If you pray, you can ask Allah for courage.

wordCard.voice: Fudul: the virtuous, or the excellent, the name of the Meccan pact to stand with anyone wronged, which the Prophet witnessed as a young man. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: hilf, a pact or alliance; al-fudul, often rendered the virtuous or the excellent.

carryVoice: Your line: defend the wronged. Tomorrow, the trustworthy. Day seven hundred fourteen, done.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the Hilf al-Fudul at the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an; 'I would not exchange it for red camels')
Later sirah tradition, e.g. Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kabir (the unpaid trader from Yemen; his cry from the hill; the debtor made to pay)
Qur'an 4:135 (stand firm for justice, as witnesses for Allah, even against yourselves or your kin)
